assumptions.summary: Rider health and safety are represented by speed, energy, and aggression upper limits, although numerical limits are not supplied.
Secondary factors such as rider equipment are omitted to focus on rider type.
The course is divided into flat, uphill, downhill, and sharp-corner segments using slope and curvature thresholds.
Riders are assumed to act fairly and perform to the best of their ability.
Wind speed and direction remain fixed within each short segment and only the longitudinal wind projection is modeled.
The drag coefficient remains fixed because rider posture is assumed unchanged.
Section equations use steady speed and omit acceleration, drivetrain loss, braking, and wheel inertia.
Team riders share a common speed; the leader bears most drag and follower aerodynamic drag is removed in the extension.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: CyclingTips and Olympics web pages are cited for course, weather, and environmental conditions without packaged route files or access dates.
Table 1 supplies qualitative traits for specialist, climber, sprinter, rouleur, and puncheur rider types.
The rider test protocol calls for three to five full-power efforts of different durations with at least one hour of recovery.
The selected fit emphasizes severe and extreme power-duration domains based on cited physiology/model-comparison literature.
Figure 5 provides an example scatterplot and 3P-CP fit with goodness of fit 0.864, but not raw points or fitted parameters.
Table 4 fixes a female rider at 165 cm, 55 kg, Pmax=990 W, Wprime=550 J, CP=230 W, and BC=0.87 for course control variates.
Tokyo input tables provide temperature, pressure, altitude, wind, humidity, rolling coefficient, density, and drag coefficient.
Flanders input tables provide a second environment/route bundle and eight calculated course sections.
The self-designed route provides a map, elevation profile, weather table, and resistance constants but no coordinates or segment table.
Table 13 reports exact/estimated sensitivity values, COV, and error rates for five rows despite prose declaring four xi factors.
Table 14 reports a four-strategy by three-terrain failure-probability matrix without trajectory definitions or replicate design.

models.summary: Eq.1 maps total work and time to AP; MMP remains indexed by effort duration.
Eq.2 gives the finite-Pmax 3P-CP curve; Eq.3 provides a simplified Wprime backcalculation.
Eq.4 defines Fr as kr times normal force.
Eq.5-Eq.8 progress from still-air quadratic drag to projected relative speed and a signed cubic-over-absolute form.
Eq.9-Eq.11 map pressure/temperature, altitude proxies, height, mass, and sex to rho and Smax.
Eq.12-Eq.14 define flat and slope power balances and a corner traction/centripetal interface.
Eq.15 bundles the total-time objective, finite-power constraints, MMP function, fourth-power NP, and AP.
The prose reconstructs sensitivity as a partial derivative of conditional failure probability with respect to xi.
The source prints a self-referential leader equation, then reports a=45%, b=85%, and c=130% for a three-phase schedule.

weaknesses.summary: The notation table prints the natural-logarithm base as e=2.178 instead of approximately 2.718.
The notation table gives air density in g/L while course tables use kg/m3 and does not reconcile the scales.
R is reused across ideal-gas and pressure-altitude formulas without distinguishing universal and specific gas constants.
Bike-control ability BC lacks a stable definition, unit, normalization, and empirical calibration across the paper and Memo.
The statement that CP power is sustainable all the time overstates the finite physiological meaning of critical power.
The example fit reports only goodness 0.864; fitted CP, Pmax, Wprime, raw points, residuals, uncertainty, and holdout results are absent.
The claim that riders spend 40 percent of full power overcoming rolling and wind resistance is unsourced and scenario-dependent.
Eq.6-Eq.8 omit yaw/lateral aerodynamics and give an angle-based sign explanation that does not match the relative-speed sign formula.
Eq.9 omits air molar mass and Kelvin conversion; Eq.10 misdescribes pressure variables and has an unresolved constant/units route.
Eq.11 does not disclose the Stevenson formula's input units, source calibration, or reason for the one-quarter multiplier.
Eq.12-Eq.13 assume steady force-power balance and omit acceleration, braking, drivetrain efficiency, and wheel inertia.
Eq.14 uses sqrt(Fr^2-Fc^2), which can become imaginary and has no justified tire-traction interpretation.
Eq.15 contains unexplained or weak constraints, an arbitrary 1.15 MMP factor, and no complete link from Pi to vi/ti in the displayed program.
The paper calls scipy SLSQP gradient descent and treats the best of a finite set of local optima as a global optimum without proof.
Initial values, multi-start count/distribution, random seed, tolerances, constraint residuals, stopping rules, runtime, and code are absent.
Table 4 reports Wprime=550 J, an implausibly small anaerobic work reserve unless the unit or value is misstated.
Five rider types in Table 1 become four in Figure 10 and three directions in the Memo without a documented mapping.
The plus/minus 10 percent and greater-than-90-percent compliance claims do not identify actual observations, metric, sample, or uncertainty.
The sensitivity method omits the failure event, distributions, thresholds, subset levels, sample count, estimator, and repeat uncertainty.
Table 13 mixes derivative estimates, COV, error rate, and failure probability; it contains a fifth row omitted from the declared x1-x4 factors.
Start-fast, start-slow, and keep-changing strategies are not defined quantitatively or controlled for work, so Table 14 is not reproducible.
The printed team equation Pleader=c*Pleader is self-referential; surrounding prose suggests Pleader=c*PITT.
Followers are modeled with aerodynamic drag removed rather than reduced, and drafting coefficients or spacing are absent.
The team solve omits rider fatigue states, transitions, drop constraints, fourth-finisher timing, objective details, and solver diagnostics.
The body assigns one strongest-stamina rider to lead the final 15 percent, while the Memo assigns two all-round riders to alternate.
The humid-track recommendation for thick, high-friction tires is not supported by the model and may conflict with reduced rolling resistance.
Table 3 prints the AP and NP formulas in the opposite indicator rows, while Eq.15 uses the conventional assignment, creating an internal metric conflict.
Eq.15 does not visibly bind Pi, vi, and ti to the section force equations, slopes, radii, or segment parameters, leaving the optimization apparently underconstrained.
Figure 8 calls the layout four course types but renders only three subfigures; the third is labeled Downhill while showing centripetal-force content associated with a corner.
Table 13 defines x1-x4 in prose but includes x5, and x3's exact -0.002215 versus estimate -0.2219 differs by roughly 100x despite a reported 0.18 percent error.
The team instruction to ignore formula (9) cannot itself remove aerodynamic drag because Eq.9 defines density; the follower zero-drag interpretation is therefore not mechanically traceable.
Wprime=550 J implies only about 1.83 W above CP under the Memo's five-minute test relation, suggesting a scale/unit or transcription problem.
Figure 10's caption reverses the described left gender-comparison and central type-comparison panels.
Reference [2] contains a literal line-break slash, reference [8] has a duplicated numeric prefix, and several page ranges are concatenated, weakening source traceability.
The extracted text contains encoding corruption in prose, so formula and visual claims must be anchored to rendered PNGs rather than text bytes alone.
